title: Broken Wrist After a Fall: Will a Plaster Do, or Do I Need a Plate?
seoTitle: Broken Wrist: Plaster or Surgery? What the Evidence Shows
metaDescription: Many broken wrists heal well in a plaster, especially after 60. When a cast is enough, when a plate or wires help, what trials show and how long recovery takes.
intro: A fall on an outstretched hand, a swollen wrist and an X-ray showing a break at the end of the forearm bone (the distal radius): this is one of the most common fractures we see, particularly in women over 50. The first question most people ask is whether they need an operation. Often the honest answer is no — but not always, and the reasons are worth understanding before you decide.
summary: Not always. Many wrist fractures heal well in a plaster, and in adults over about 65 large trials have not shown that surgery gives a better wrist a year or two later. Surgery is more often advised for younger, active people and for breaks that are badly displaced, unstable or run into the joint.

sections.heading: Does every broken wrist need an operation?
sections.body: No. If the broken bone is in a good position, or can be pushed back into place and held there, a plaster cast is usually enough. Surgery is used when the bone cannot be put back properly without an operation, or will not stay in place in a cast. For many older adults with lower demands on the wrist, a cast is a reasonable choice even when the bone is not perfectly aligned. AAOS OrthoInfo notes that some older adults may not even need the bone straightened.

sections.heading: How does the doctor decide between a plaster and surgery?
sections.body: There is no single rule. The decision balances the X-ray against the person:
bullets: How far the bone has shifted, and whether it can be put back and held in a cast
Whether the break runs into the wrist joint surface, where a step can matter more
Your age, which hand it is, and what you need the wrist for — work, sport, two-wheeler riding, household tasks
Bone strength, other health conditions and how safely you can have an anaesthetic
Whether the skin is broken over the fracture, or the nerves in the hand are affected — these change the urgency

sections.heading: I am over 60 — is a plaster really as good as a plate?
sections.body: For many people, yes. In the WRIST trial (JAMA Network Open, 2021), adults aged 60 or over with unstable wrist fractures were treated with a plate, other forms of fixation or a cast. At 24 months there was no meaningful difference in patient-reported hand function between the groups. The bone more often healed slightly out of position in the cast group, but this did not translate into a worse result for patients overall. The AAOS plain-language guideline summary states that patients over 65 may not benefit from surgery, and that closed reduction and casting may be better for this age group. One honest caveat: in WRIST, patients chose casting rather than being randomly assigned to it, so the comparison with surgery is not perfectly balanced.

sections.heading: What if the bone slips while I am in the plaster?
sections.body: This is the main risk of choosing a cast, and the reason follow-up X-rays matter. A fracture can be well aligned on day one and drift over the next two to three weeks. AAOS OrthoInfo describes X-rays every week for the first three weeks and again at six weeks for fractures at risk of moving. In the DRAFFT2 trial, 33 of 255 people treated in a moulded cast (about one in eight) needed an operation because the fracture position was lost in the first six weeks. So starting in a plaster does not close the door on surgery; it means keeping your follow-up appointments.

sections.heading: When is surgery the better choice?
sections.body: Surgery, usually with a plate and screws or with wires, is more often advised for younger, active adults, for breaks that are badly displaced or unstable, for fractures that disturb the joint surface, and when the bone cannot be held in a cast. The AAOS guideline summary reports moderate-strength evidence that adults under 65 benefit from operative treatment. Open fractures (where the bone has broken the skin) and fractures with nerve problems are treated urgently. Surgery brings its own risks, so it should be chosen for a clear reason rather than by default.

sections.heading: How long until my wrist works normally again?
sections.body: The cast usually comes off about four to six weeks after the injury. According to AAOS OrthoInfo, most wrist fractures take about three months to heal enough for all everyday activities, and full recovery can take up to a year. Almost everyone has some stiffness, which keeps improving for at least two years; in some people, especially after a severe break or over the age of 50, a little stiffness is permanent. Moving the fingers from the start, and wrist exercises once the cast is off, help recovery.

sections.heading: Why should my bones be checked after a wrist fracture?
sections.body: A broken wrist from a simple fall at standing height can be the first sign of osteoporosis. AAOS OrthoInfo notes that one fragility fracture almost doubles the risk of another, and that your doctor may recommend testing your bone strength. A bone density (DEXA) scan and treatment, if needed, can lower the chance of a more serious fracture later, such as a broken hip.

sections.heading: When should I go to emergency straight away?
sections.body: Go to an emergency department promptly, rather than waiting for a clinic appointment, if:
bullets: Your fingers are numb, tingling or pale
The wrist looks badly bent or out of place
The pain is severe, keeps getting worse, or is severe when someone gently straightens your fingers
The skin over the break is cut or the bone is visible
You have new weakness or difficulty bending the thumb or index finger

faqs.q: Does a broken wrist always need surgery?
faqs.a: No. If the bone is in a good position, or can be put back and held there, a plaster cast is usually enough. Surgery is used when the bone cannot be realigned or will not stay in place in a cast, and more often in younger, active adults.

faqs.q: Is a plaster as good as a plate for a broken wrist in older people?
faqs.a: For many adults over 60 to 65, yes. The WRIST trial found no meaningful difference in hand function at 24 months between plates, other fixation and casting, and the AAOS guideline summary states that patients over 65 may not benefit from surgery.

faqs.q: Can I still need surgery after being put in a plaster?
faqs.a: Yes. Some fractures slip in the first few weeks, which is why X-rays are repeated. In the DRAFFT2 trial, about one in eight people treated in a moulded cast needed surgery because the bone moved in the first six weeks.

faqs.q: How long does a broken wrist take to heal?
faqs.a: The cast usually comes off after about four to six weeks. Most wrist fractures heal enough for all everyday activities in about three months, and full recovery can take up to a year. Some stiffness is common and keeps improving for at least two years.

faqs.q: Should I have a bone density test after breaking my wrist?
faqs.a: If the wrist broke in a simple fall, often yes. It can be the first sign of osteoporosis, and one fragility fracture almost doubles the risk of another. Ask your doctor whether a DEXA scan is appropriate for you.
